prize_parts.citation: for an oeuvre that remakes the boundaries between lyric, essay, translation and narrative through a lifelong dialogue with the classical tradition

statement.case_for: Anne Carson has a very distinctive voice that joins classical scholarship, lyric, narrative and visual or book-object form. Autobiography of Red and Nox are the works the list names. As far as public knowledge shows, her formal invention comes out of a long engagement with the literary tradition and is not novelty for its own sake. Her voice is recognisable across genres, and her method has been consistent over several decades, which supports sustained quality. The case for her rests on distinctiveness of voice, formal achievement and imaginative range across the whole body of work. After reading colleagues' openings I still place her first, as a literary judgement and not as a response to the opening tallies.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one Anne Sward raises: whether the oeuvre is a consistent literary architecture or a series of brilliant experiments. Much of her best-known work is hybrid and idiosyncratic. It leans on classical learning, and its reception is concentrated in Anglophone literary culture. Book-object and visual forms also travel poorly in translation, so a committee reading in several languages may judge her unevenly. Her breadth may not match the intensity of her best-known books. I cannot resolve this from public knowledge alone, and I have not verified a full reading of the corpus.

responses.point: Sward ranks Carson fifth. She finds the formal invention and voice distinct, but holds tentatively the worry that the work may be inventive but niche. She also notes that dependence on classical knowledge may narrow its significance, and she is unsure how to weigh performance and book-object forms in an oeuvre assessment.
responses.response: I take this as the right test, and I do not think it is settled. I would answer in part that the classical engagement is a through-line of method and not a barrier to entry. It recurs across poetry, essay, translation and the verse-novel as a way of asking how old forms and stories carry present feeling. Treating that recurrence as one project argues for architecture over a string of experiments. I concede the risk is real, and that book-object works such as Nox are the hardest to judge as literature from text alone. I would weight the verbal and narrative achievement over the object form, and I do not claim the question is closed.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first as the strongest case on formal and linguistic achievement. He cites the remaking of Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and argument with inherited forms, the extension of that work into critical essays, and a fully formed oeuvre of lasting influence.
responses.response: I agree that the criteria Olsson names, formal and linguistic achievement, voice and intellectual depth, are the right ones, and Adonis meets them seriously. I ranked him fourth, and that difference is mostly about evidence. His case depends on Arabic prosody, diction and intertextual work that the committee, as Olsson himself says, can judge only partially through translation. I would not downgrade him for that, and it is why he remains a serious alternative for me. Carson's formal achievement is more directly open to English-language readers, though the same translation caveat applies to how widely the committee can judge her across languages. I also agree with Olsson that his political positions should stay out of the literary judgement.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for dense, visionary Romanian prose in Blinding and Solenoid. She finds the voice highly recognisable and the formal ambition sustained over long, architecturally complex books. Her concern is whether the later volumes keep the same intensity and whether the self-referential scale blurs the distinctness of individual books.
responses.response: I agree on the strength of the case and ranked him third. Blinding and Solenoid show ambition, formal control and imaginative range, and I name him as my first alternative. I share Mattson's concern, and my own reservation is excess and repetition within the largest works. That bears on sustained quality, and I cannot test it here. Carson's work is smaller in scale, which makes it easier to judge for consistency, though it also raises the breadth question. I would be willing to move toward Cărtărescu if the discussion clarifies how the later volumes compare with the earlier ones.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first on distinctiveness of voice and sustained inventive reach. He also asks whether the metaphysical scale is matched by emotional and moral range, and he is cautious about how translation affects sentence-level effects.
responses.response: The question about emotional and moral range is a fair one, and I think it applies to every candidate who works at cosmic scale, not only Cărtărescu. I read the lyrical and bodily intensity of the prose as a sign of human depth, but I cannot confirm that across the corpus. His poetry is the part least accessible to non-Romanian readers, so the committee's view of the whole oeuvre may be incomplete, which is a limit on how firmly any of us can argue the point.

uncertainties: My assessment of Carson rests on public knowledge and not on verified reading of the full corpus.
It is unclear whether the breadth of her oeuvre matches the intensity of its best-known works, and whether the whole is a consistent architecture or a series of experiments.
Hybrid and book-object forms may lose much in translation, so the committee's coverage of her work may be uneven.

The translated coverage and quality of Adonis, Can Xue and Cărtărescu, whom I name as alternatives or rank highly, limits how securely any of us can compare the formal achievement of the original-language works.
It is uncertain how the translated corpora of the leading candidates compare in sustained quality across their later work.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My biographical and critical work on Selma Lagerlöf, my collaboration with Kate Larson and my election alongside David Håkansson have no documented connection to any shortlisted writer. My own literary practice is context and not evidence of a preference.
